title: Felt very exploitative. Instant delete.
body:
Before I could even see the app, I was shown a subscription screen. I tapped the X because I wanted to explore the product before paying. Instead of taking me to the app, it presented another sales screen stating: “This offer only appears once. Grab 40% off before it’s gone.”

I found this use of artificial urgency very exploitative. It pressures users to make an immediate purchasing decision before they can evaluate what they are buying. This is particularly troubling in an ADHD-focused app, since ADHD can involve impulsivity and difficulty making decisions under pressure.

The very next screen prompted me to rate the app, although I still had not seen or used it. That screen also advertised “Over 30,000 five-star reviews.” Requesting ratings before users have experienced the product undermines their credibility and makes me question how meaningful those reviews are.

An app claiming to support people with ADHD should hold itself to a much higher ethical standard. I deleted it immediately.

title: Heading in the wrong direction
body:
I’m using Tiimo begrudgingly and out of desperation. 

On one hand, it’s the only app I’ve managed to find that offers the niche functions I need: task management, time blocking, live activities and Apple Watch complications, and focus timers that automatically start at scheduled times. It allows me to plan my day in advance and reduce the friction of having to make in-the-moment decisions the following day, which is a big help for folks with ADHD. I can easily see what I should be doing at any given moment and how long I have left to do it. So yeah—kudos to making my days a bit easier.

On the other hand, the Tiimo team seems to be going in a direction that many users, myself included, don’t actually want—any amount of online research will reveal similar sentiments.

1. It’s clear that they’re trying to force users to use their AI assistant. From any tab in the app (including the focus timer), the purple assistant icon stares at you, begging to be clicked. On top of the icon, you’ll sometimes see a banner in the Today tab when you open the app, prompting you to plan your day with the assistant. I don’t doubt that it might be useful for some users, but why not provide the option to hide/toggle it off or at least put it in its own tab? The extra UI clutter for a feature that should be discretionary and the fact that the team is so heavy-handed with their promotion of it isn’t very ADHD-friendly. 

2. The ability to create and save custom routines is unclear. From the Today view, you have the option to explore routines from your recent tasks (those with sub-task) or select one from a library of premade routines. However, there’s no guidance about what a routine actually is in the context of the app and how to actually create one in a way that’s modular and intuitive. Your best bet is creating a to-do item with sub-tasks and then having it repeat, choosing a preset, or asking the chat assistant to help you.

3. Their website (not the web app) seems to bombard you with popups to subscribe to Pro each time you navigate to a new page. Being a paid subscriber who sometimes wants to just browse their resource or product pages, the popups are already quite irritating. But for a potential user looking to spend money and commit to a new app, the frequent interruptions are pushy and distracting—two things that set off alarm bells for someone with ADHD.

I really want to like Tiimo and use it long-term, which is why I put all this effort into typing up my feedback in the first place. I can largely ignore or overlook most of the issues I have with the app, and I believe the Tiimo team generally does care about supporting people with ADHD. 

But the app’s lack of flexibility and choice when it comes to their AI tool is a red flag for me—it points to a possible business-driven desire to be competitive in the AI space which, at least in my case, comes at the expense of user agency, needs, and preferences. I’ll likely stick with Tiimo until something better comes along, but I’m pessimistic about the direction the app’s development will take.

title: Close but not there yet
body:
There’s a big opportunity in the task management space: to leverage magic (AI) to help organize and de-clutter our busy lives. 

There’s a ton of “dumb” to-do list apps out there. Some have tried to grab the opportunity (Motion is one) but no one has succeeded. The main reason is that managing the app ends up feeling like work by itself. 

I had high hopes with Tiimo. On the surface it offers it all: beautiful UI, thoughtful UX, and an assistant that is suppose to auto-magically help you manage your list. 

The problem is that it doesn’t do that, so the whole promise falls apart. The AI-assistant is simply not good enough and so Tiimo ends up being just another to-do list to manage. I found it too frustrating to use. The assistant in Motion, despite its other flaws, did do something well: it gives ppl what they want: super simple and a zero-effort way to make sense of what to do next.

If Tiimo can greatly improve the assistant and offer us a magical “schedule my whole week” button…and does it intelligently, I would use the app all the time. I hope future updates improve this as I really believe it is trying to tackle a real and meaningful problem.

I heavily relied on the time-based aspect for large routines (e.g. a morning routine) which was fantastic when used with my Apple watch. It was a massive game changer in terms of not losing track of time or tasks that needed to be done in a time crunch as a neurodivergent person. Their newest forced update to routines is frankly horrible, they’ve turned robust routines with timed aspects and notifications into a checklist - making this no better than writing down a list. I had a busy, time-sensitive morning routine all planned out for today and woke up to see it had turned into a checklist in the app, which was extremely jarring to say the least. I used to love this app but considering its geared toward neurodivergent folks, they sure do love to make massive design overhauls or change the entire system constantly which is a little ironic considering many neurodivergent people struggle with change and/or rely on routine heavily. Because of this latest update it looks like I’ll be cancelling my subscription after nearly 5 years, and going back to an old fashioned checklist. RIP to what was once the best planning app I’d ever used.

title: Inclusive Intentions, But Falls Short for Visually Impaired Users
body:
I was initially excited about the potential of the Tiimo app, hoping it would assist me, a neurodiverse individual, in organizing my day and breaking down tasks. However, my experience was hindered by the app's lack of accessibility for visually impaired users.

Despite the developers' emphasis on intersectionality, the app falls short in catering to the needs of individuals with visual impairments. The absence of compatibility with Apple's built-in accessibility features for the blind, such as font size adjustments, makes the app unusable for those who rely on these features.

While the developers advocate for intersectionality, they seem to overlook the reality that many individuals face multiple disabilities, both physical and neurodiverse. The visually appealing design of the app contrasts sharply with its inaccessibility to visually impaired users, reinforcing the exclusionary nature of technology for those with diverse disabilities.

As someone who is Non-Binary, Mad, Neurodiverse, Chronically Ill and Visually Impaired, I find it disappointing that an app claiming to champion intersectionality neglects a significant portion of its potential user base. The review serves as a call to action for developers to align their words with meaningful steps towards inclusivity for ALL. 

Anybody who may be looking for an app like Tiimo that is accessible to those who are Low Vision or Blind, check out the Structured app. From the start, their app has been accessible to those most marginalized by inaccessible technology. 

Do better.

title: Extremely Disappointing -an autistic habit & schedule app explorer
body:
I had high hopes due to it being marketed towards people like me (Autism, ADHD, and more) and I’m now deleting it more disappointed than i expected. This app has been much more difficult to use as an auDHD person than others i’ve tried. It absolutely has potential, but its currently too flawed, disorganized, complex, visually unappealing to be worth using imo.

1. My Day and Library don’t seem to be synced, in that deleting something in one doesn’t delete it in the other, so theres no actual way to see a list of all of your routines & activities.

2. Editing an activity in the Library will create a duplicate in both the library and the day planner which you have to individually delete.

3. Editing a routine in My Day will create a duplicate in My Day that doesn’t show up in the routine Library.

4. There’s no separation between repeating activities/routines and one time activities/routines in the Library, so activities like “feed the cat” or “do laundry” will be mixed in with “watch star wars” or “stitch hole in jeans” from 3 months ago. It’s more of a history tab than a library.

5. Activities and Routines take up an unnecessary amount of space in My Day to the point where you can only see maybe 2 on your screen at once. Routines particularly have huge chunks of unnecessary empty space both when theyre expanded and when theyre collapsed.

6. No transition between activities & routines in My Day. Its just block after block. An example of good visual transitions between events can be found in an app called Structured, which will remain my primary app despite having less features.

7. You can only ever see the plan for one day at a time, ie theres no way to get a glance at the coming week (i expected this to appear in the top bar of the My Day page when i added tasks but it didn't)

8. Glitches. A lot.

and more, but I can’t remember them. Bye!

title: The idea is there, but not executed well…
body:
The idea of this app is great, especially for someone with adhd, however there are some major flaws that make it frustrating to use. Honestly unless they fix the issues, it’s not worth using. 

It’s great for planning your day and setting reminders for tasks. I often find it hard to manage my time and don’t realize how long specific tasks take. The app was great to help me plan my mornings to ensure I have enough time to get everything done before work. However, if you set a time for a task, the app automatically checks the task off even if you haven’t completed and won’t let you uncheck it if it’s in a routine, so then I’m scrambling trying to fix it, getting flustered, ultimately making my adhd worse. 

Solution: only allow tasks to be checked off manually once user actually completes them. If the task takes longer than intended, let it go into overtime. We are not robots and it is normal to run a few minutes or seconds behind…

title: Thank you from the bottom of my heart ❤️
body:
This app helped me so much in such a short period of time! It made me « see » time. I have never been able to incorporate time into my perception of the world and organize myself with it. In my mind, I have all the time in the world or none at all at the same time. 

The day after setting up my routines and activities, I arrived at work 20 minutes in advance and I didn’t have to run to get there! Just casually walk! It NEVER happens!

It was amazing to feel the weight of the stress I felt since I was little finally being lift off of my shoulders.

Using it made me able to do the amount of tasks I usually do in three weeks, in only three days! It’s amazing! It really keeps me focus and motivated and it is really satisfying to check the tasks that are done. I still can’t estimate the time it will take me to do a series of tasks, but I can with one and the app calculates the total of them together so I can organize myself to finish at the right time and not be late.

I discovered that I probably have ADD (not sure for the « H ») with an article on their blog. Now, I can go and get tools to improve my life with that information.

It’s cliché, but this app changed my life in the best way possible as I am struggling to organize myself starting a business to teach gardening while working 40h/week.

It is a great tool, and the people behind it do it with passion and it shows. I was won over by their ethics when I read that they didn’t put adds in for a free version because it defied the purpose of the app and that they are trying to keep it as low of a price as possible so that more people can use it while they can provide for themselves as a company. I applaud this!

Please continue your great work! It is trully helpful.

Thank you! Thank you! Thank you!

title: Almost perfect although a couple of bugs/suggestions
body:
As a person with ADHD I actually really like this app. It helps me keep track of the tasks that absolutely need to be done each day. That is what I use it for. There are a couple of things that I wish could be included in this app or adjusted. 

For one I would like there to be an Apple Watch complication that didn’t involve me having to open the app on Apple Watch. Even just the emoticon or title of your next task on your watch screen all the time would be super helpful. I personally need reminders to start these things because I’m constantly thinking of other things and incredibly forgetful so having it front and centre every time I looked at my watch would be super helpful. 

Also I’ve had issues where tasks that don’t have specific start times do not show up on the iOS widget until you actually start them. I would like it just to show me the tasks that I have to do whether they have a specified start time or not. The majority of my day the widget says well done even though I have not completed the tasks that I have set for that day. It would also be nice to have an option of the smaller square widget and not just the medium one. 

Other than that it’s a great app and I totally recommend it.
